article.Citation/Title: Heinzerling, K. G., Sergi, K., Linton, M., Rich, R., Youssef, B., Bentancourt, I., Bramen, J., Siddarth, P., Schwartzberg, L., & Kelly, D. F. (2023). Nature-themed video intervention may improve cardiovascular safety of psilocybin-assisted therapy for alcohol use disorder. Frontiers in Psychiatry, 14, 1215972.
article.SourcePDF: alcohol/Heinzerling, K. G., Sergi,. Nature-themed video intervention.pdf
article.Outcome: Visual Healing < Standard (lower peak post-psilocybin increase in systolic blood pressure during Week 3 session)
article.InterventionDescription: Two open-label 25 mg oral psilocybin sessions 4 weeks apart plus weekly counseling; participants randomized to nature-themed Visual Healing video versus standard eyeshades-and-music set-and-setting during dosing.

ae_events.Description: Headache, most frequent AE (16 total: 5 Visual Healing, 11 Standard), possibly/probably/definitely related to intervention (Table 3).
Elevated blood pressure (10 total: 3 Visual Healing, 7 Standard), a monitored vital-sign AE during psilocybin dosing (Table 3).
Nausea (8 total: 2 Visual Healing, 6 Standard), possibly/probably/definitely related to intervention (Table 3).
Twitching (5 total: 2 Visual Healing, 3 Standard) (Table 3).
Anxiety (4 total: 3 Visual Healing, 1 Standard), listed as an AE but may overlap with expected in-session challenging-experience phenomenology (Table 3).
Feeling flushed (3 total, all 3 Visual Healing, 0 Standard) (Table 3).
Tachycardia (3 total, all Standard, 0 Visual Healing), monitored vital-sign AE (Table 3).
Abdominal pain (1, Standard group) (Table 3).
Body aches (1, Standard group) (Table 3).
Bradycardia (1, Visual Healing group), monitored vital-sign AE (Table 3).
Depressed mood (1, Standard group) (Table 3).
EKG abnormality (1, Visual Healing group), monitored during dosing session; no clinical intervention described (Table 3).
Insomnia (1, Standard group) (Table 3).
Low blood pressure (1, Visual Healing group), monitored vital-sign AE (Table 3).
Synesthesia (1, Standard group), a classic acute perceptual psilocybin effect (Table 3).
Jaw clenching/pain (1, Standard group) (Table 3).
Tinnitus (1, Standard group) (Table 3).
Tremor (1, Visual Healing group) (Table 3).
Vivid dreams (1, Standard group) (Table 3).
Vomiting (1, Visual Healing group); occurred at conclusion of Opening Video, participant unsure if video or medication contributed, did not recur Week 7.
Wooziness (1, Standard group) (Table 3).
Serious Adverse Event: severe alcohol intoxication requiring Emergency Department treatment, Week 2, prior to any psilocybin dosing.
Serious Adverse Event: severe alcohol relapse requiring inpatient detoxification admission, Week 6, causing study discontinuation.

article.Outcome: The article's Study endpoints section (2.3) lists FOUR co-equal primary endpoints -- recruitment/retention, minutes of Visual Healing viewed, adverse events, and vital signs -- assessing feasibility/safety/tolerability, with alcohol-use outcomes explicitly designated secondary and 'psychedelic effects, anxiety and stress' exploratory. Per the boundary case for trials whose SUD outcome is secondary, Outcome is coded to the stated PRIMARY domain rather than the alcohol-use secondary outcome. Among the four co-primary domains, 'vital signs' produced the only statistically significant between-group primary-endpoint result and is the finding the title, abstract, and Discussion foreground: peak post-psilocybin increase in blood pressure was significantly lower for Visual Healing vs Standard (Results 3.2.2, Figure 4A). Systolic BP (chi2(1)=4.98, p=0.02) is selected over diastolic BP (chi2(1)=4.03, p=0.04) per the 'largest among co-equal primaries' tie-break rule, since both are the same primary domain (vital signs) and SBP has the larger test statistic; this tie is flagged as a judgment call. No numeric group means/SDs for the BP change itself are printed in the body text -- the only quantitative values given are the Kruskal-Wallis chi-square and p; the underlying means are shown only in Figure 4A, whose OCR/markdown conversion rendered as unusable garbled 'picture text' glyphs, so no numeric magnitude is fabricated for Outcome. IMPORTANT DISCREPANCY: this is a cardiovascular safety comparison between two psilocybin-exposed arms (Visual Healing vs Standard set-and-setting), not a substance-use outcome and not a psychedelic-vs-non-psychedelic comparison -- flagged per task instructions for human review before this is treated as an AUD treatment-effect size on any forest plot.
article.SD: chi2(1) = 4.98 is the Kruskal-Wallis test statistic explicitly paired with the Outcome direction/finding in Results 3.2.2 ('systolic BP: Kruskal-Wallis test chi2(1) = 4.98, p = 0.02'); df=1 is printed explicitly by the authors (not inferred). The diastolic BP statistic (chi2(1)=4.03, p=0.04) and heart rate statistic (chi2(1)=2.78, p=0.10, non-significant) are alternative vital-sign parameters from the same analysis, not used here because SBP was selected as primary per the Outcome rationale.
article.SampleSize_NFinal: 20 = all randomized participants (10 Visual Healing + 10 Standard) who underwent the Week 3 psilocybin dosing session, which is the specific comparison analyzed for this primary vital-signs endpoint ('analyses are focused on the Week 3 psilocybin session in which participants were randomly assigned to the Visual Healing versus Standard procedures,' Section 2.3). No attrition before the Week 3 session is reported (the one dropout occurred later, in Week 6), so N=20 is used rather than the 19-completer final sample.

MethodologyDescribedYN.note: All 14 elements are explicitly described. objective/outcomes: Section 2.3 lists primary/secondary/exploratory objectives and instruments. design: pilot RCT of a video intervention within open-label psilocybin therapy (Methods, para 1). setting: Pacific Treatment & Research in Psychedelics Program clinic, Santa Monica, CA. eligibility: detailed inclusion/exclusion criteria (Section 2.1). intervention: Visual Healing video protocol (Section 2.2.2). comparator: Standard eyeshades/music procedures (Section 2.2.4). sample_size_power: N=20 justified by feasibility/budget rationale (Methods para 1), and the study's underpowered nature for detecting clinical differences is explicitly acknowledged in Limitations ('adequately powered to detect potential differences ... are needed'), which satisfies the criterion even without a formal a priori power calculation. randomization: randomization list generated in advance and held by a staff member without participant contact (Section 2.2.1). blinding: explicitly described as absent -- 'lack of blinding with the video intervention' (Limitations) -- satisfies the criterion since description-of-absence counts. statistical_methods: Kruskal-Wallis, Fisher's exact, and mixed-effects repeated-measures models specified (Section 2.4). results: full Results section with tables and figures. harms: AE assessment protocol and Table 3 (Section 3.1.2). funding_coi: separate Funding and Conflict of interest sections both present and substantive. n_met=14 >= 13, so MethodologyDescribedYN=1.

article.Pos Result Y/N: 1. The trial's stated primary endpoints (feasibility, safety, tolerability) were all met positively: 95% retention, no video-related AEs, and Visual Healing additionally showed a favorable safety signal (significantly smaller peak BP increase vs Standard). The secondary AUD outcome also improved: drinking days and heavy drinking days decreased significantly and were sustained through 14 weeks in both arms, and PROMIS Alcohol Use scores decreased significantly (F(4,18)=12.9, p<0.0001). No true non-psilocybin control exists, so this reflects the intervention's own pre/post direction rather than a placebo-controlled AUD efficacy claim.
article.RandomizationYN: 1. Randomization applied to the Visual Healing vs Standard set-and-setting assignment for the Week 3 session (not to psilocybin vs placebo, since all participants received open-label psilocybin). Coded 1 because a genuine randomization procedure was used for the trial's controlled comparison, per Section 2.2.1.
article.BlindingYN: 0. The video intervention could not be blinded to participants or the two-clinician team present in the dosing room; the article states this explicitly as a limitation ('lack of blinding with the video intervention').
article.MediatingYN: No formal mediation analysis (indirect-effect test, Baron-and-Kenny sequence, causal mediation model) was conducted. The Discussion narratively hypothesizes that Visual Healing 'might improve psychedelic therapy by reducing participants' anxiety' and speculates anxiety reduction underlies the BP finding, but no formal test of this mechanism was run (STAI/cortisol were tested as separate parallel exploratory outcomes, not as mediators of the BP effect). Coded 0, not 3, because a plausible mediator (anxiety/cortisol) was in fact measured.
article.ModeratingYN: No formal interaction/moderation test was reported. The Discussion and Figure 4B/Supplementary Figure S4B compare Week 3 vs Week 7 cardiovascular/anxiety trajectories for the subset of Standard-group participants who did or did not choose to view the video in Week 7, but this is described as 'visual inspection of plots' with explicit caveats about 'small number of participants and lack of random assignment,' not a formal subgroup-by-treatment interaction test. Coded 0 per the rule that side-by-side subgroup reporting without an interaction test is 0, not 1.
article.HypothesisTestReportedYN: Coded 1: the primary vital-signs comparison reports Kruskal-Wallis χ² statistics with p-values (SBP χ²(1)=4.98, p=0.02; DBP χ²(1)=4.03, p=0.04), Results 3.2.2.
article.Power: 1. No a priori power calculation is reported, but the Limitations section explicitly states additional 'adequately powered' studies are needed, which is a bare acknowledgment that the current pilot was underpowered -- this satisfies the field per the rule that a bare underpowered statement counts as 'discussed'.
article.Retention (%): 95 = 19/20, stated directly in the Abstract and Results ('Nineteen of the 20 (95%) randomized participants ... completed the 14-week study'). Denominator is the randomized N (20), which equals the enrolled/eligible N here since eligibility screening preceded randomization with no separate enrolled cohort reported.
article.BaseStatus: 'Severe' -- Table 1 reports AUD severity as Moderate 2/10 (VH) + 5/10 (Standard) = 7/20 (35%) and Severe 8/10 (VH) + 5/10 (Standard) = 13/20 (65%); Severe is the plurality/majority category for the pooled sample. Judgment call to summarize a mixed distribution into a single closed-enum value.
article.Age_Median: '30-50'. Abstract reports overall mean age 49 +/- 11 years for study completers, which falls in the 30-50 bracket (consistent with the rule that a mean of 48.5 maps to 30-50). Table 1 per-arm means (46.9 and 51.0) straddle the boundary but the reported overall figure (49) is used.
article.RaceEthnicity_BIPOCPercent: 5 = 1/20, from Table 1's 'Asian & Native Hawaiian or Pacific Islander' row (1/10 Visual Healing, 0/10 Standard), the only non-White racial category reported. Hispanic ethnicity is reported separately and inconsistently crosses race (1/10 Hispanic in each arm = 2/20 = 10%), but Table 1 does not indicate whether these 2 Hispanic participants fall within the White or Asian/NHPI racial rows, so they are not added to the 5% figure -- flagged as an ambiguity per the codebook's guidance on Hispanic ethnicity crossing racial categories.
article.RecruitmentRepresentYN: 0, judgment call. Recruitment channels were broad (fliers, public radio, clinician/treatment-program referral, website), but the eligibility funnel was highly restrictive: only 20/55 (36%) of consented candidates were eligible, with exclusions for any other current psychiatric disorder (including nicotine/drug use disorder), most psychiatric medications, significant cardiac/hepatic/neurological/endocrine disease, and psychosis/bipolar history -- comorbidities common in real-world AUD populations. This narrows the sample well below a representative clinical AUD population.
article.Followup in months: 1. Counseling/treatment concluded at Week 10; the dedicated follow-up assessment occurred at Week 14 (Section 2.2.5), i.e., 4 weeks (~1 month) after end of treatment. Per the rule to measure from end-of-treatment rather than from baseline/randomization (which would be ~14 weeks, ~3.2 months) when both horizons are reported, the shorter post-treatment interval is used.
article.QualityOfLifeMeasured: 0, judgment call. No dedicated quality-of-life instrument was administered. The Persisting Effects Questionnaire includes one item on 'personal well-being and life satisfaction' (Table 5), but this is a single retrospective item within a psychedelic-effects questionnaire, not a validated QoL measure, so it is not counted as QoL being explicitly measured.
article.RelapseMeasured: 1, judgment call. Relapse/return-to-use was not tracked via a dedicated instrument, but one participant's 'severe alcohol relapse' was explicitly identified, named, and tracked as the cause of a Serious Adverse Event and study discontinuation (Section 3.1.2), which constitutes relapse being explicitly tracked as an outcome of clinical significance.
article.ArmScope: 'psychedelic_arm'. Unlike a typical psychedelic-vs-placebo trial, both study arms (Visual Healing and Standard) received identical open-label 25 mg psilocybin dosing -- the randomized factor is the video/set-and-setting intervention, not psilocybin exposure itself. All 20 participants in Table 3's AE counts are therefore psilocybin-exposed, so 'pooled' (which requires mixing exposed and unexposed participants) does not apply. Caveat: the Week 2 Serious Adverse Event (severe alcohol intoxication, AE23) occurred before this participant's own first psilocybin dose, but this does not change the article-level classification, which reflects the overwhelmingly psilocybin-exposed AE dataset in Table 3.
article.NumDistinctAEs: 23 = 21 distinct AE types listed in Table 3 ('Frequency of adverse events rated as possibly, probably, or definitely related to study interventions') plus 2 additional distinct Serious Adverse Events described separately in prose (Section 3.1.2: severe alcohol intoxication requiring ED treatment; severe alcohol relapse requiring inpatient detoxification), which are alcohol-related medical events not attributed to study intervention and therefore not included in Table 3's intervention-related AE list.
article.NParticipantsWithAE: '.' -- the article reports per-AE-type counts (Table 3) and a total AE count (63) but never states the number of unique participants with >=1 AE; this cannot be derived from per-type counts without risking double-counting participants who had multiple AE types.
article.EligibleYN: Y. (a) Clinical trial: prospectively planned, IRB-approved, FDA IND-covered pilot RCT with defined enrollment, randomized assignment (video intervention), and prospective outcome assessment through Week 14 -- passes. (b) SUD outcome: alcohol use (drinking days, heavy drinking days per week via Timeline Followback, and PROMIS Alcohol Use Short Form T-scores) is reported as a secondary outcome with explicit statistical results (Section 3.2.1) -- passes, per the rule that trials whose only SUD outcome is secondary remain eligible. Note per task instructions: the article's STATED PRIMARY outcome domain is feasibility/safety/tolerability (a cardiovascular-safety finding drives the headline result), not the substance-use outcome -- this discrepancy is recorded here and reflected in the Outcome field per the boundary-case rule.
article.SchemaRevisionNote: 2026-09-03 schema-revision splice: ConfoundYN/PVal removed, MediatingYN/ModeratingYN/HypothesisTestReportedYN added, sourced from a separate v3 extraction run (PromptVersion v1.3) rather than this file's own v1.2 run. Every other field in this file is unchanged from the original v1.2 extraction -- this file is now a hybrid of two runs for these 3 fields only. See clinical_adjudication.md '2026-09-03 -- Coding-scheme revision' for the full rationale.

ae_events.Heinzerling 2023_AE02: Elevated blood pressure is a vital-sign AE captured via the described 30/60/90/120min,4/6/7h monitoring protocol during the 7-hour dosing session; the article states BP/HR 'had returned to normal levels by the end of the seven-hour post-dosing observation period,' supporting in-session onset and Mild severity (no rescue medication given per 'No participant received rescue medications during the trial').
ae_events.Heinzerling 2023_AE05: Anxiety is listed as a study-intervention AE in Table 3, but psychedelic-session anxiety is also expected challenging-experience phenomenology (CEQ-sense); coded AE_type='both' per the rubric's instruction to flag rather than silently absorb such events into a purely clinical AE count. No escalation, rescue medication, or persistence beyond the session is reported, so Mild.
ae_events.Heinzerling 2023_AE11: Depressed mood's onset timing relative to the dosing session is not specified in the article; unlike the vital-sign AEs, this is plausibly a post-session/delayed phenomenon rather than an in-session one, so Onset is coded 'unknown' rather than assumed.
ae_events.Heinzerling 2023_AE13: Insomnia plausibly manifests after discharge (participants were monitored in-clinic for ~7 hours, typically 9am-4pm) rather than during the described in-session monitoring window; no explicit timing is given, so Onset is coded 'unknown' rather than assumed in-session.
ae_events.Heinzerling 2023_AE19: Vivid dreams plausibly occur during post-session sleep rather than the in-clinic monitoring window; no explicit timing given, so Onset is coded 'unknown'.
ae_events.Heinzerling 2023_AE20: Vomiting has specific narrative detail (Section 3.1.2): occurred 'at the conclusion of the opening video,' i.e., during the dosing session, supporting in-session onset; the participant was 'unsure if the video or the medication had contributed more' and chose not to view videos in Week 7, after which no vomiting recurred -- included for context though not required by any field.
ae_events.Heinzerling 2023_AE22: Authors explicitly label this a 'Serious Adverse Event' (SeveritySource='author'), so Severity='Severe' per rubric precedence (author-assigned seriousness overrides rubric grading). Onset is coded 'unknown' rather than a dosing-relative category because this event (Week 2, ED treatment for severe alcohol intoxication) occurred BEFORE this participant's first psilocybin dose (Week 3) -- none of in-session/post-session-acute/delayed cleanly describes a pre-exposure event. MeetsFDASerious='Y' (ED/inpatient-level treatment); InterventionRequired='Y' (ED treatment). Article notes 'no indication the relapse was due to study participation' for the participant's overall course.
ae_events.Heinzerling 2023_AE23: Author-labeled Serious Adverse Event (SeveritySource='author'), Severity='Severe'. Onset coded 'delayed' (weeks+) because this event occurred in Week 6, approximately 3 weeks after the participant's Week 3 psilocybin dosing session. MeetsFDASerious='Y' and InterventionRequired='Y' (inpatient alcohol detoxification admission, resulting in study discontinuation). Article states the participant 'has a history of multiple prior inpatient alcohol treatment episodes and there was no indication the relapse was due to study participation.'

config_proposal.note: chi2(1)=4.98, N=20 meets the 1-df chi-square conversion requirement and is mathematically convertible via phi=sqrt(chi2/N). Downgraded from 'clean' to 'approx' because this is a cardiovascular-safety comparison (peak systolic BP increase) between two arms that BOTH received active open-label psilocybin -- it is not a psychedelic-vs-non-psychedelic AUD treatment-effect comparison, and its direction/sign relative to 'favors treatment for AUD' is not well-defined. A human reviewer should decide whether this study's stated-primary safety endpoint belongs on an AUD-focused Tier-1 forest plot at all, versus using the secondary alcohol-use finding (no significant between-group difference; both arms improved similarly over time with no placebo control) instead.
